newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu to present 1997 budget cuts Monday.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu to present 1997 budget cuts Monday.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor issued a joint appeal to ministers to support further cuts in the 1997 budget to be presented to the government on Monday.

The two held meetings on Sunday with key coalition partners to persuade them to drop their opposition to budget cuts on top of the 4.9 billion shekels ($1.32 billion) of cutbacks included in the Treasury's original 1997 budget.
Treasury sources put the additional cuts at some 1.8 billion shekels ($486 million).

"We will present tomorrow the budget proposals to cut the deficit which do not include raising taxes or imposition of additional taxes," Netanyahu told a news conference. He added it was "always possible" to raise taxes in the future.
"I ask for your understanding and your support."

Treasury sources said while the proposals did not call for tax hikes, they included other methods to raise revenues including the sale of government-owned homes in Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Israel's state-owned Channel One television said some 3,000 housing units could be sold. The move would be certain to infuriate Palestinians, who hope to build an independent state in the territories Israel seized in the 1967 Middle East war.

Netanyahu said the defence budget would not be reduced but declined to say where the cuts would fall. The proposals face strong opposition in Netanyahu's government and in parliament on the grounds that they would fall hardest on the disadvantaged.
Treasury sources said the proposals would pare specific sums from ministry budgets while leaving ministers the power to allocate the cuts.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, a champion of the underprivileged, declined to say if he would support the cuts.
"I do not want to say anything until the discussion is wound up," Levy said, adding his Gesher faction had to maintain its "credibility and commitment" towards low-income groups.
Netanyahu met with Education Minister Zevulon Hammer, who strongly opposes cutbacks in education, late on Sunday.
The budget was due to be presented to the government ON Monday morning. If ratified, it will be sent to parliament for approval.
